R6.3.response:
You are right, and the measurement is worse than your estimate. We have turned the objection into a contribution rather than softening the claim.

Over a 60,000-flow stream at 99.998 percent attack prevalence, the alert rate is 0.99997, so the policy of the submitted paper does attribute essentially every flow. Classification alone sustains 35,715 flows per second at 0.028 milliseconds per flow. One TreeSHAP attribution costs 1.485 milliseconds, so the unbudgeted pipeline sustains 661 flows per second, a factor of 54 below the classification rate. The 1,953 flows per second reported in the submitted manuscript was optimistic by roughly a factor of three.

The revision defines the explanation trigger formally as a separate admission decision rather than a consequence of the prediction, and measures three budget policies against it. The one that works is not a faster explainer. It is a trigger that distinguishes an alert from an episode: structurally identical flood flows are one attack, so one representative is attributed and every other alert in the episode carries an explicit reference to it, which keeps the audit trail complete while the number of TreeSHAP evaluations falls.

How far it falls depends entirely on how an episode is defined, and this is the part we did not anticipate. Our first signature included per-flow volume terms, which fragmented the flood into 53,817 episodes and recovered almost nothing, a factor of 1.1. A signature on the target address and protocol collapses the same stream to two episodes, a reduction of thirty thousand, and restores 35,652 flows per second, which is the classification rate to within 0.2 percent. A token-bucket budget makes the opposite trade, keeping full per-flow fidelity for a fixed number of alerts per second: at 50 explanations per second it sustains 33,273 flows per second with 0.14 percent of alerts individually attributed. Asynchronous off-path attribution is the weakest of the three, because a queue large enough to avoid drops moves the bottleneck without relieving it.

We state the cost of the policy that works rather than presenting the throughput figure alone. A coarse episode explains why a flood against a given service is being blocked. It does not explain why one particular flow within that flood scored as it did, and an analyst investigating a suspected false positive needs the latter. The policy is therefore a scale control to be tightened as alert volume falls, and the reported frontier is what lets an operator choose the point rather than discover the cost in production.
R6.3.action: Defined the explanation trigger formally as an admission decision, measured the unbudgeted collapse, and measured episode deduplication at three granularities, a token-bucket budget at six rates and asynchronous off-path attribution at three queue depths, reporting the throughput-versus-coverage frontier and the interpretive cost of the policy that recovers the most throughput.
R6.3.location: Sec. VII-K (The cost of explanation, and how to bound it) and Table 13, Algorithm 1 and Sec. IV, Sec. IX-C (Deployment considerations)
